title: Blockchains & Verifiable Computation
subtitle: A Lumenary CS elective: how blockchains reach agreement without a central authority, and how cryptographic proofs let anyone check a computation without redoing it.
description: This elective of [Lumenary CS](/en/cs/) teaches two connected ideas. A **blockchain** is a ledger kept by many parties who do not trust one another, and it raises hard questions in distributed systems, cryptography and economics. **Verifiable computation** asks how one party can prove to another that a computation was done correctly, with a proof far quicker to check than the computation itself; its zero-knowledge proofs and SNARKs began as theory and now run in production, in blockchains and beyond.

The course assumes Lumenary CS up to the Engineering level — above all [applied cryptography](/en/cs/applied-cryptography/) and [replication and consensus](/en/cs/replication-and-consensus/) — and some comfort with modular arithmetic ([Lumenary Math](/en/math/) has it). Code is in Python, and every block with a **Run in browser** button runs there: you will build a Merkle tree, mine a toy chain, sign with Schnorr signatures and run the sumcheck protocol yourself. Smart-contract code in Solidity is shown and explained, not run.

It is written to inform, not to sell: nothing here is investment advice, and the lessons are as plain about fraud, failures, energy use and open problems as about what works. Every lesson was drafted with AI assistance and is awaiting review by a human expert. The text, exercises and code are original and licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 (code Apache-2.0); papers, specifications and projects' own documentation are linked, not retold.

levels.title: Trust, cryptography and consensus
levels.summary: Why anyone would want a blockchain, and the pieces it is built from: trust models, hash functions and Merkle trees, digital signatures, and the two families of consensus, proof of work and proof of stake.

levels.title: Blockchains in practice
levels.summary: How real chains work and fail: Bitcoin's transactions, Ethereum and smart contracts, contract security and MEV, scaling with rollups and data availability, and an honest look at applications, limits and regulation.

levels.title: Verifiable computation
levels.summary: Proofs that a computation was done correctly, checkable far faster than redoing it: interactive proofs and sumcheck, zero knowledge, arithmetisation and SNARKs, STARKs and folding, zkVMs and coprocessors, and the research frontier.
